title_tag: Potassium Foods and Blood Pressure: What to Eat
og_title: Potassium-Rich Foods and Blood Pressure: What to Eat
desc: Potassium-rich foods help balance sodium and relax blood vessels. Here's which foods have the most, how much you need, and who should be careful.
subhead: Potassium helps your kidneys flush out extra sodium and eases tension in blood vessel walls. Here's which foods actually deliver it, and where the evidence stops.
alt: Assortment of potassium-rich foods including bananas, spinach, beans and sweet potatoes on a counter
takeaways: Potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relax vessel walls, which is why potassium-rich diets are consistently linked to lower blood pressure.
Bananas aren't the top source. White beans, potatoes with the skin on, spinach and lentils all carry more potassium per serving.
The updated daily target is about 3,400 mg for men and 2,600 mg for women, per the National Academies' 2019 guidance, lower than the older 4,700 mg figure still quoted online.

pull: Potassium doesn't cancel out a high-sodium diet. It works alongside cutting sodium, not instead of it.
body: Potassium helps the body flush out excess sodium through urine and eases tension in blood vessel walls, which is why diets rich in potassium are consistently linked to lower blood pressure. Bananas get most of the attention, but white beans, leafy greens, potatoes with the skin on and plain yogurt often carry more potassium per serving. For most healthy adults, food sources beat supplements.

The sodium-potassium relationship is one of the more solid findings in nutrition research, even though the two minerals get covered very unevenly. Most public health messaging focuses on cutting sodium; potassium is the quieter half of the same equation, and raising it is one of the more reliable, low-risk ways to support healthy blood pressure alongside sodium reduction, not as a replacement for it.
How does potassium affect blood pressure?

Potassium helps your kidneys excrete sodium more efficiently, which reduces the fluid volume your blood vessels have to handle. It also appears to ease tension in the smooth muscle lining blood vessel walls, letting them relax slightly rather than staying constricted. Together, these effects show up in research as a modest but real reduction in blood pressure, more pronounced in people with higher sodium intake and in people with existing hypertension than in people who already eat a lower-sodium, higher-potassium diet.

This is also the mechanism behind the DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension), which pairs lower sodium with higher potassium, calcium and magnesium through fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low-fat dairy. DASH has some of the strongest clinical trial evidence of any dietary approach to blood pressure, and potassium-rich foods are a core part of why it works.
Which foods have the most potassium?

Bananas are the cultural shorthand for potassium, but they're mid-pack compared with several less-hyped options. Figures below are approximate USDA values per typical serving; treat them as a guide to relative ranking, not an exact target.

Beans, lentils, leafy greens and potatoes with the skin left on consistently rank near the top of USDA food composition data. A diet that includes a few of these most days gets you much closer to the daily target than relying on bananas alone.
How much potassium do you actually need per day?

The figure that circulates most online, 4,700 mg a day, is outdated. The National Academies updated the Dietary Reference Intakes in 2019 and set the Adequate Intake at about 3,400 mg a day for adult men and 2,600 mg for adult women, based on a review that found the older number wasn't well supported by evidence of added benefit above that level. Most adults in the US still fall short of even the newer, lower target, largely because processed food is high in sodium and low in potassium-rich whole foods.

You don't need to track milligrams daily to benefit. Building most meals around at least one potassium-rich food, a side of beans, a baked potato with the skin, a serving of leafy greens, moves the average up without any math.
Can you get too much potassium from food?

For someone with healthy kidneys, it's hard to overdo potassium through food alone; the kidneys adjust excretion well within a wide range, and whole foods release potassium gradually during digestion. The risk picture changes sharply for people with reduced kidney function, since impaired kidneys can't clear potassium efficiently and blood levels can climb to dangerous ranges, which can affect heart rhythm. That risk applies much more to supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes, which deliver a concentrated dose quickly, than to spreading potassium-rich foods across meals.
Are potassium supplements a shortcut worth taking?

Generally, no, not without medical guidance. Over-the-counter potassium supplements are capped at low doses in the US precisely because high-dose potassium taken quickly can be dangerous, particularly for anyone with kidney issues or on certain medications. Potassium-based salt substitutes (often labeled "lite salt") deliver a meaningfully higher dose per use than people expect and have caused serious problems in people who didn't realize they were also on a potassium-sparing medication.

If a doctor has diagnosed you with low potassium (hypokalemia), they may prescribe a supplement at a specific dose and monitor your blood levels. That's a different situation from choosing to self-supplement for blood pressure, which isn't well supported and carries more risk than simply eating more beans, greens and potatoes.
Does cooking method change how much potassium you actually get?

Yes, more than most people expect. Potassium is water-soluble, so boiling vegetables and then pouring off the water takes a meaningful share of the mineral with it. Potatoes boiled in large amounts of water, for example, lose more potassium than potatoes that are baked, roasted or steamed. Canned beans and vegetables are a reasonable shortcut, but rinsing them doesn't remove much potassium since it's bound inside the plant tissue, not just sitting in the liquid.

If you want to get the most out of a potassium-rich food, lean toward baking, roasting, steaming or microwaving over boiling, and use any cooking liquid in a soup or sauce rather than draining it away. None of this makes a dramatic difference on its own, but it adds up over a week of meals the same way the food choices themselves do.
Does age or salt sensitivity change how much this helps?

Not everyone's blood pressure responds to sodium and potassium the same way. Some people are considerably more "salt-sensitive" than others, meaning their blood pressure moves more in response to sodium intake. Older adults, people with obesity, and people with existing high blood pressure tend to fall into this more sensitive group on average, which also means they may see a more noticeable benefit from pairing lower sodium with higher potassium. People who are less salt-sensitive may see a smaller effect, but the overall dietary pattern is still considered heart-healthy for other reasons, so it's rarely a reason to skip it.

There's no simple home test for salt sensitivity, so this isn't something to self-diagnose. It's more useful as context for why two people can follow the same advice and see different results on a home blood pressure monitor.
Does the sodium-to-potassium ratio matter more than potassium alone?

Some researchers argue the ratio between sodium and potassium intake predicts blood pressure outcomes better than either mineral measured alone, since the two work through overlapping kidney and vascular pathways. In practical terms, that supports doing both things at once: trimming processed, high-sodium foods while adding potassium-rich whole foods, rather than treating them as separate projects. Our guide on lowering blood pressure naturally covers the sodium side of this in more depth.
How does potassium compare with just cutting salt?

Cutting sodium and raising potassium both move blood pressure in the same direction, and most trial evidence suggests doing both produces a bigger effect than either alone. Sodium reduction tends to have a somewhat larger average effect in people eating a very high-sodium diet to begin with. Potassium's advantage is that it's an easier habit to build: adding beans to a meal is a smaller behavior change for most people than relearning how they season everything.
Neither replaces the other. A diet that's still high in sodium but technically "potassium-rich" is not the same as a genuinely heart-healthy pattern; the two need to move together.
Who should be careful with potassium-rich foods?
A few groups should talk to a doctor before deliberately increasing potassium intake, especially through concentrated sources like salt substitutes or supplements:
People with chronic kidney disease, who often need to limit potassium rather than add more, since impaired kidneys can't clear it as well.
People taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics (such as spironolactone), which can raise blood potassium levels on their own.
People on certain heart medications, where high potassium can affect heart rhythm; this is a conversation for a cardiologist, not a label.
Anyone with a history of hyperkalemia (high blood potassium), diagnosed by bloodwork, not symptoms alone.

None of this means avoiding potassium-rich food. It means the "more is better" instinct that applies to most healthy adults doesn't apply the same way to these groups, and a blood test, not a guess, should guide how much they eat.
What if you don't like beans or leafy greens?

Plenty of potassium-rich foods have nothing to do with kale or lentils. Dairy and dairy alternatives fortified with potassium, citrus fruit, melon, tomatoes and tomato sauce, squash, and dried fruit like apricots and prunes all rank well. A cup of tomato sauce carries a surprising amount, which is part of why pasta night with a vegetable-forward sauce isn't a bad choice for this specific goal, even though it rarely gets mentioned next to spinach and beans.

The point isn't to force down a food you dislike. It's to notice that potassium shows up in more places than the usual short list, so there's almost always a version that fits what you already enjoy eating.
What does a potassium-rich day of eating actually look like?

You don't need a special diet plan, just a habit of including a potassium-dense food at most meals. A realistic day might run: oatmeal with a banana at breakfast, a lentil or bean-based salad with spinach at lunch, a baked sweet potato or regular potato with the skin at dinner alongside a vegetable, and plain yogurt or an orange as a snack. That pattern alone, done most days, gets a lot of people closer to the daily target without counting a single milligram.

Pair it with the broader habits that support blood pressure generally, regular movement, enough sleep and limiting processed food, rather than treating potassium as a standalone fix. Our piece on walking and heart health covers the exercise side of that picture, and our guide to resting heart rate by age is a useful way to track whether these habits are moving the needle over time. faq: Can bananas alone lower blood pressure?

Not on their own in any meaningful way. A single food rarely moves blood pressure; it's the overall pattern of potassium-rich, lower-sodium eating over weeks and months that's linked to a real effect.
Is coconut water a good source of potassium?

It has some, typically around 400 to 600 mg per cup depending on the brand, comparable to a banana or an orange. It's a reasonable option but not dramatically higher than whole foods, and it often costs more per milligram of potassium.
Do potassium supplements work as well as food for blood pressure?

There isn't strong evidence they work better, and they carry more risk of overshooting safe levels quickly. Most guidance favors getting potassium from food unless a doctor has diagnosed a deficiency and prescribed a specific dose.
Does cooking reduce the potassium in vegetables?
Boiling can leach out some potassium into the water, especially if you discard the cooking liquid. Steaming, roasting or microwaving generally retains more than boiling does.
Is a low-sodium diet enough on its own, without adding potassium?
It helps, but most trial evidence suggests combining lower sodium with higher potassium produces a bigger effect on blood pressure than cutting sodium alone.
How fast does increasing potassium intake affect blood pressure?

Some studies show measurable changes within a few weeks of sustained higher intake, though individual response varies with baseline diet, kidney function and other factors. It's not an overnight effect.
Can you get enough potassium without eating bananas at all?
Easily. Beans, lentils, leafy greens, potatoes with the skin and yogurt all supply as much or more potassium per serving, so skipping bananas changes nothing if you're eating a varied diet.
